title: Phase 10 · Stage 30 (boss): Write the tests yourself
summary: Prove the domain works with your own checks: value objects, policies, and a whole lend-and-return story driven by a ManualClock.

steps.title: Tests are code you keep
body: For 29 stages the dojo has checked your work. A real team checks its own, and the tests stay in the codebase so the next change cannot quietly break an old rule. You already have the harness the dojo uses; now you write the checks:
Dojo.Eq("Standard fine for 5 days late", new Money(2.50m), Policies.Standard.FineFor(5));
Dojo.Check("an address with two @ is rejected", Email.TryCreate("a@@b.com") is null, "it was accepted");

A good test has three parts, **arrange, act, assert**, and tests **one behaviour** with a name that says which. Stage 24 is what makes the Library testable at all: give it a `ManualClock` and fresh in-memory repositories, and a three-week story runs in microseconds:
var library = new Library(clock, new SequentialIdGenerator(), new InMemoryRepository<Book, string>(), ...);  // arrange
Dojo.Eq("returned 6 days late", 6, library.Return("1", grace.Id).Value!.DaysLate);                        // assert
Test the edges as well as the happy path: zero, the limit, one past the limit, the error kinds.

steps.prompt: Arrange the test in arrange, act, assert order.
lines: var second = library.Lend("1", ada.Id); // the only copy is already out
Dojo.Eq("a second loan of the only copy is a Conflict", ErrorKind.Conflict, second.Kind);
steps.explain: Build the world, do the one thing being tested, then check the outcome.

steps.prompt: Which test name is the most useful when it fails?
options: `"Premium members pay nothing for the first 2 days late"`
steps.explain: A failing test should tell you which rule broke without opening the code.

steps.prompt: Your test passes, then you break `PremiumPolicy.FineFor` on purpose and it **still** passes. What does that tell you?
options: The test does not actually check the behaviour it is named after
The policy was not really broken
Tests should not be run twice
The compiler cached the old code
steps.explain: Breaking the code on purpose to watch a test fail is how you test your tests. A test that cannot fail protects nothing.

steps.title: ShelfwiseTests
prompt: At the very end of the file add:

**Run checks** calls `Shelfwise.Tests.ShelfwiseTests.Run()` first, so every `Dojo.Eq` / `Dojo.Check` / `Dojo.Throws` you write becomes a row, and then re-checks the API over HTTP. Write **at least 12** checks, all passing, that cover:
1. `Money`: adding, and that a negative amount throws (`Dojo.Throws`).
2. `Email`: normalising (`"  Ada@Example.COM "` becomes `ada@example.com`) and at least one rejection.
3. Both policies: a Standard fine, the Premium grace days, and the 10.00 cap.

4. A **Library** built in the test with its own `new ManualClock(...)` and fresh repositories: a successful loan and its due date, a second loan of the only copy failing with `ErrorKind.Conflict`, an unknown member failing with `ErrorKind.NotFound`, and, after `clock.Advance(...)`, a late return with the right days late and balance.

? string.Join(",", json.EnumerateArray().Select(e => DojoWeb.Prop(e, property)))

require.message: The tests build their own ManualClock

hints: A helper keeps the arranging short: `static Library NewLibrary(IClock clock) => new(clock, new SequentialIdGenerator(), new InMemoryRepository<Book, string>(), new InMemoryRepository<Member, int>(), new InMemoryRepository<Loan, int>());`.
`Dojo.Eq` compares with `Equals`, so `Money` and `DateOnly` values compare directly: `Dojo.Eq("due in 14 days", new DateOnly(2026, 3, 16), loan.Value!.DueOn);`.

The story: add one book with 1 copy, join a Standard member, lend (success), lend again (Conflict), lend to member 99 (NotFound), `clock.Advance(20)`, return: 6 days late and `library.BalanceOf(id)` is `new Money(3m)`.
